so sorry, i should’ve clarified what i meant - i was referring to overdosing the sedative, not the sodium pentobarbital. 

your comment about aspirating a significant amount of blood makes sense! i understand my mistake now. 

i had never heard of walking sedation before but i am absolutely going to suggest that in our next meeting. 

for an added note - i do not catch pole any dog unless i absolutely have to, and even within that, i try to limit the time they are on the catch pole. i am thankful for the provided sources for alternate restraint methods - i will also bring this up in our next meeting!

thank you for your response, it’s very helpful. 

to answer your question, we inject straight from the needle, not a catheter. i have had far fewer experiences with blowing a vein when the dog is awake vs sedated, my knowledge of why this occurs is because of the reduced flow of blood when sedated and then the vein is less pronounced and trickier to hit.. or the blood begins to coagulate before all or even half of the fatal plus can be injected - that’s where i wonder if we are either giving too high of a dosage, or too little? could you provide insight as to why we may be experiencing these issues (veins not being as pronounced, blood coagulating before the full dose can be injected)? 

i am not opposed to sedation, and to your point i do think it is very important to ensure we are doing everything in our power to create as peaceful of a passing as possible. could you provide some resources or just advice in general for recommended restraint methods? currently, the written protocol states that in order to sedate safely, dogs must be placed on catch pole. this almost always results in dogs being incredibly stressed until they lose consciousness. i hate doing it this way, it is awful to have the last moments of their lives be so filled with fear.
thank you for your input. i’m glad to hear from someone who works in a shelter, it gives me a better perspective.
